frozen_original.synopsis: China's retaliatory tariffs in 2025 reduced U.S. agricultural exports to China from $24.5 billion in 2024 to just $8.4 billion in 2025, a two-thirds decline and the lowest annual figure in over two decades, per NDSU Agricultural Trade Monitor analysis. NDSU estimated the annualized China-specific agricultural export shortfall at $14.9 billion — 41% larger than the $10.6 billion shortfall during the 2018–2019 trade war. Soybeans accounted for $6.8 billion of the loss; beef and cotton each contributed $1.3 billion; corn $333 million; and tree nuts $964 million. For the first time in more than 20 years, Chinese importers purchased no soybeans from the U.S. autumn 2025 harvest, forcing American farmers to store their crops as prices fell to a five-year low. Brazil's soybean exports to China hit record levels in 2025, topping 85 million metric tons — an 18% increase — as U.S. market share evaporated.
frozen_original.title: Agricultural Sector Devastated: China Soybean Exports Collapse 72%, $14.9B Loss

proposal.description_long: A May 2026 report by North Dakota State University researchers assessed the effects of China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural exports. Using a structural gravity model, the authors estimated an annualized $14.9 billion shortfall in U.S. exports to China over March 2025 through February 2026, relative to a 2024 export baseline. The report attributes the modeled shortfall to China’s Fentanyl and Reciprocal tariff layers and estimates that soybeans account for about $6.8 billion. It also explains that the model separates tariff effects from other influences, including global commodity trends, exporter and importer shocks, seasonality, and monthly aggregate shocks. The figure is an estimate of China-bound export sales, not a direct measure of net harm to U.S. farmers. The report does not support the source record’s claim of a 72% soybean-export collapse. The AgEcon Search record dates the report to May 19, 2026, so this proposal treats the item as report-publication context and corrects the March 4, 2025 record date rather than presenting the later estimate as known on that date.
proposal.description_medium: A May 2026 North Dakota State University report estimates that China’s retaliatory tariffs reduced U.S. agricultural exports to China by $14.9 billion on an annualized basis during March 2025–February 2026. The model assigns about $6.8 billion of the shortfall to soybeans. These are estimates of China-bound exports and a modeled tariff effect, not measured net losses to farmers or a 72% soybean-export collapse.
proposal.description_short: A May 2026 NDSU report estimates China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs cut U.S. agricultural exports by $14.9 billion annualized.

staged_record.description_long: Reuters reported on August 13, 2025, that Chinese buyers were booking soybean cargoes from Brazil for shipment during a key U.S. marketing period, leaving U.S. exporters at risk of missed sales while trade talks continued. Traders said buyers had secured about four million metric tons for October, roughly half of expected requirements, from South America. Reuters noted that U.S. shipments to China typically occur from September through January before Brazilian supplies take over after the South American harvest. Traders said late-year or early-2026 U.S. sales might still occur, but could be limited if tariffs remained. These bookings support a description of a seasonal shift in prospective soybean sales. They do not substantiate the supplied account’s later full-year agricultural-export shortfall, its $14.9 billion figure or a 72% soybean figure. The packet also dates this entry March 4, 2025, months before the Reuters article. That chronology must be resolved before this report can be attached as evidence for the dated event.
staged_record.description_medium: Reuters reported on August 13, 2025, citing traders, that Chinese buyers were booking Brazilian soybeans for a key supply period while U.S. exporters risked missing sales. Traders said China had secured about four million tons for October from South America. This supports a seasonal account, not later full-year export totals or the title’s 72% figure. The packet dates this record March 4, 2025, before the cited report.
staged_record.description_short: Reuters reported Brazilian cargo bookings were filling China’s soybean demand during the U.S. 2025 marketing window.
